title: if I do ... and if I did ...
subtitle: if we take the bus / if we took the bus
summary: Use if + present for things that may really happen, and if + past with would for things that will not happen or that you don't expect to happen.

lesson.heading: Two ways of talking about the bus

left.label: If we take the bus ... (possible)
left.text: Lisa and Jess are deciding how to travel. For Jess, it is possible that they will take the bus, so she uses if + present.
examples: *Lisa:* Shall we take the bus or the train? *Jess:* **If we take** the bus, it **will be** cheaper.

right.label: If we took the bus ... (not going to happen)
right.text: Later, Lisa and Jess decide to take the train. Now Jess knows they are not going to take the bus, so she uses if + past.
examples: *Joe:* How are you going to travel? *Jess:* We're going to take the train. **If we took** the bus, it **would be** cheaper, but the train is quicker.

lesson.heading: if + past for things that will not happen
lesson.text: When we talk about something that will not happen, or we don't expect that it will happen, we use **if + past** (if we went / if there was etc.). But the meaning is not past - we are imagining a situation now or in the future.

examples.text: What would you do **if you won** a lot of money?
examples.note: I don't really expect this to happen

examples.text: **If there was** an election tomorrow, who would you vote for?
examples.note: there will not be an election tomorrow

examples.text: I'd be surprised **if they didn't come** to the party.

lesson.heading: if I find or if I found?

left.label: if I find (a real possibility)
examples: I think I left my watch at your house. **If you find** it, can you call me?

right.label: if I found (an imagined situation)
examples: **If you found** a wallet in the street, what would you do with it?

lesson.heading: No would in the if-part
lesson.text: We do not normally use **would** in the if-part of the sentence. The if-part takes the past form.

examples.text: I'd be very scared **if somebody pointed** a gun at me.
**If we went** by bus, it would be cheaper.

lesson.heading: would in the other part
lesson.text: In the other part of the sentence (not the if-part) we use **would ('d) / wouldn't**.

examples.text: **I'd be** scared if somebody pointed a gun at me.
I'm not going to bed yet. I'm not tired. If I went to bed now, **I wouldn't sleep**.
What **would you do** if you were bitten by a snake?

lesson.heading: could and might
lesson.text: **Could** and **might** are also possible in the main part of the sentence. Could means 'would be able to', and might means 'it is possible that ... would'.

examples.text: If I won a lot of money, I **might buy** a house.
examples.note: = it is possible that I would buy a house

examples.text: If it stopped raining, we **could go** out.
examples.note: = we would be able to go out

lesson.text: Ask yourself: do I think this will really happen? Yes - use if + present and will. No, or probably not - use if + past and would.

exercises.prompt: You're not going to sell your car because it's old and not worth much. Which do you say?
options: If I sold my car, I wouldn't get much money for it.
If I sell my car, I won't get much money for it.
If I would sell my car, I wouldn't get much money for it.
exercises.explanation: You are not going to sell the car, so you imagine it: if + past (sold) and wouldn't in the other part.

exercises.prompt: Be careful with that vase. If you ___ it, it would break into small pieces.
exercises.explanation: You are imagining something that you don't expect to happen, so use if + past: if you dropped it.

exercises.prompt: You often see Sarah. A friend of yours wants to contact her. Which do you say?
options: If I see Sarah, I'll tell her to call you.
If I saw Sarah, I'd tell her to call you.
If I'll see Sarah, I'll tell her to call you.
exercises.explanation: You often see Sarah, so it is a real possibility: if + present (see) and will in the other part.

exercises.prompt: Does the speaker think the situation is possible, or is it something they don't expect to happen?

items.text: If we take the bus, it will be cheaper.
If we took the bus, it would be cheaper.
If you find my watch, can you call me?
If you found a wallet in the street, what would you do?
I'd be surprised if they didn't come to the party.
If you go right at the end of this street, you'll see a bank.

exercises.prompt: I can't afford to buy a car. If ___ a car, I'd have to borrow the money.
exercises.explanation: An imagined situation: if + past (I bought) with would in the other part.

exercises.prompt: If you had a party, who ___?
exercises.explanation: The if-part has the past (had), so the question part uses would: who would you invite?

exercises.statement: I'd be very scared if somebody would point a gun at me.
exercises.explanation: I'd be very scared if somebody pointed a gun at me. We don't normally use would in the if-part.

exercises.prompt: Match each if-part with the result that goes with it.

pairs.left: If I won a lot of money,
If I went to bed now,
If somebody pointed a gun at me,

exercises.prompt: I don't think Gary and Emma will get married. ___ amazed if they did.
exercises.explanation: I don't expect it to happen, so use would in the main part: I'd be amazed.

exercises.prompt: We're not going to stay at a hotel. (it / cost too much) Write a sentence beginning If ...
exercises.answer: If we stayed at a hotel, it would cost too much.
exercises.explanation: We are not going to stay at a hotel, so: if + past (stayed) and would in the other part.

exercises.statement: If it stopped raining, we could go out.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Could is possible instead of would here: we could go out = we would be able to go out.

exercises.prompt: Kevin is not going to apply for the job. (he / not / get it) Write a sentence beginning If ...
exercises.answer: If he applied for the job, he wouldn't get it.
exercises.explanation: Kevin is not going to apply, so we imagine it: if he applied ... he wouldn't get it.
